questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: Opportunity to learn the language

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For me it was first and foremost Spain because of the language, but I chose the city because of the size (a mix between a big and a small city) and the area and the nature around.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was relatively easy to access. But the information comes from a lot of sources (UCPH, the host university, Erasmus etc) and you have to fill in information and upload documents on different websites (campus virtual and aula virtual from the University of Almería, and also mobility online). This can be quite confusing both in the proces of applying and before arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I went to the international office a couple of times to get some help with choosing subjects at the university. They were nice and helpful and I ended up choosing subjects that fit my schedule.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy on the website idealista, which had a bunch of opportunities for erasmus students. You can also look on airbnb.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In my experience, it was way better to live off campus than to live on campus. I think there are some housing opportunities on campus, but the university is placed around 6-7 km outside of the city center and you would have to take the bus or the bike all the time, because most activities take place in the city. It's way nicer to stay in city, either in the center or in the area called Zapillo. I would definitely recommend the Zapillo because it has cheap flats and rooms and it's close to the beach where most of activities take place. It's definitely possible to find a shared flat with other erasmus students or with young Spanish people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You choose the subjects before arriving, but you don't know the timetables. If you choose subjects from different semesters, you risk them overlapping and will have to change some of them. It was a bit confusing because you won't know the updated timetables for the subjects before you arrive, and the proces of changing was a bit unclear - in my experience, it wasn't clear if you had to talk to the teacher of the subject you wanted to change to before changing (and then some teachers said that they didn't know how many available spots they had in their class), or if you could just change it in your OLA. If you need to change subjects, you will most likely have a period of time where you don't have access to the subjects you want to change to in your aula virtual, which means you cannot see the homework, messages from the teacher etc. So you have to ask the students in the class to be added to WhatsApp group to know about changes in schedule etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can go to the international office at the university, but you have to make an appointment online, and the proces for doing that is very unclear on the host university's website. I had to make an appointment a couple of times because I needed to change some subjects, and every time I had to spend so much time just finding the link for making the appointment.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up registering for 5 classes that didn't overlap, but it was a bit difficult to find classes during the day that fit with each other. One of the classes I changed to ended up being very difficult if you're not a native Spanish speaker, which I would have liked to know in the beginning before choosing it and not being able to change. I just passed the subject because I did all the assignments and presentations during the semester, but the exam in itself is really, really hard. It's called Fundamentos para el Análisis y el Uso de la Lengua Española and I wouldn't recommend it to any erasmus student unless you're a native spanish speaker.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If possible, check the timetables for the subjects before choosing in the first place. It is possible to change (and maybe you'll have to anyway because you don't like the subject when you try it) but I think it would have spared me a lot of time and stress in the beginning (when everything is a bit confusing already) if I hadn't had to change because of the schedule.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In my experience as a Danish student, the work load in most of my subjects was much bigger than the work load in Denmark. Also, you don't know what the expectations are or how much you have to do to pass a subject or get a specific grade, so you would rather do everything than to risk not passing, and this ends up taking a lot of time. I had 5 subjects of 6 ECTS each, but some of them had a bigger workload than subjects I've had at UCPH of 15 ECTS. It's very different from subject to subject though. Furthermore, all my courses are in Spanish, and it's very different how much the teachers expect from you if you're not a native Spanish speaker. I talked to erasmus students that were able to do all their assignments in English, didn't have to do presentations, didn't have to take the same exams etc. so it's very different.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In a lot of subjects, it's the teacher speaking to the students without dialogue. It's basically about listening to what the teacher tells you and writing it down, so you can study it for the exams. You cannot bring anything to help you to the exams, not even your notes (some teachers allowed me to take a dictionary because of the language barrier, but others didn't), so you have to remember a lot of stuff by heart which is very different from the way they teach at UCPH. I was very scared of this beforehand but I'd say it's definitely doable if you go to the classes and then do some intense studying before the exams.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introducción a la Literatura
Fundamentos para el Análisis y el Uso de la Lengua Española
Historia de la Lingüística
Análisis Crítico del Discurso en Español
Literatura Hispanoamericana II

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you're interested in literature, I would very highly recommend taking Literatura Hispanoamericana II with the teacher Isabel. She's so kind to erasmus students (and all her students in general) and very passionate about her teaching. I love her approach to learning, which is more about actually being curious and getting to know and read a lot of amazing literature than learning a whole semester's curriculum. She does the exam at the end of the semester because she has to. You also have to read a novel in Spanish and do an oral exam about it in the middle of the semester, but if you know some Spanish it's definitely doable, and Isabel won't be to hard on the erasmus students. 

Isabel also teaches the subject Introducción a la Literatura which is a more general introduction to literature, but it's a good subject to take because the work load is not bad at all (and it's first year). 

I wouldn't recommend taking Fundamentos para el Análisis y el Uso de la Lengua Española if you're not a native Spanish speaker. The teacher Yolanda expects the exact same from the erasmus students as from the native Spanish students, so her subject's quite difficult to pass. If you do choose it, it's important to go to class because she takes 'asistencia'. 

I took Historia de la Lingüística and Análisis Crítico del Discurso en Español because they corresponded with a subject I would have had to take in Denmark (Kommunikation og formidling, 10 ECTS). Historia de la Lingüística is a good subject to take because the teacher Antonio Daniel Fuentes González is very nice with erasmus students and gives good grades if you do all of the assignments (in groups) during the semester. I did 3 out of 4 of the prácticas during the semester, and the final work (which counts as the 'exam' because the subject doesn't have a written exam of 2-3 hours in the university), and that was enough for getting a good grade. It's also important going to class. 

At first, Análisis Crítico del Discurso en Español was a bit hard because the teacher Rosario Lisciandro seemed unfriendly and to be honest a bit scary. Also apparently there was another subject in the semester before that was 'necessary' to follow this subject, so we were asked to read a whole theory book of 200-something pages from the past semester when we arrived. I ended up not finishing the book and it was fine, so don't stress too much about that. The subject is in 4th year, and therefore there are no more classes after the Easter holidays. Another pro of the subject is that there is no exam, 'only' a bunch of written assignments during the semester (but these had to be quite long and the tasks were sometimes complicated). Going to class counts quite a lot. I wouldn't recommend the subject because of the specific teacher, but it seemed like he doesn't usually teach this subject so maybe it will be someone else next year. He also talked about changing the 'exam' to an oral one, so maybe that will change too. It may be hard to avoid taking this subject if you're going on exchange on 4th semester and need 2 subjects that correspond with Kommunikation og Formidling.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I bought a bicycle which got stolen, so I had to buy another one. But later my insurance covered that. Don't place your bicycle on the street (especially not by the beach over night), even if it's locked with a strong lock. Apart from that nothing.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is definetely way cheaper than expected, both in the supermarket and when going out to eat. They have free tapas every time you order a beer at a bar or a restaurant, so you could have 3 beers and 3 tapas for 8 euros. Also housing is way cheaper than in Copenhagen. I paid 3000 DKKK (around 400 euro) for half an apartment in the Zapillo with a view over the sea and 20 meters walk from the beach, which was amazing. I know a lot of people that paid less, 200 euro-300 euro for a room for example.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The UAL have sports facilities which I know a lot of people used very often, I didn't myself but you can buy a very cheap sports card for the whole semester and then go swimming, to the fitness center etc. ESN Almería (the erasmus student organisation) also organizes a lot of activities all the time, so you have a lot of opportunities to meet new people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Just try and participate in the activities that the ESN organizes, especially in the beginning, even if it doesn't seem like your favourite activity. You meet a lot of nice people through that and then you can start organizing things on your own with them. A lot of erasmus students go to the beach a lot so you can always meet someone there.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Almería is a cute city with some cultural stuff going on. Visit the Alcazaba, the art museums, go to the theater, to Classijazz for concerts or poetry, to La Guajira for concerts, language exchange events and flamenco nights. Go out a lot to have tapas in all of the different tapas bars in the city center, especially Casa Puga, El Quinto Toro and Bar Calle de Las Tiendas, or in the Zapillo, La Cala or Café Paris. There are some nice morrocan restaurants too. Go to the beautiful natural park Cabo de Gata (either by car or take the bus to San Jose and hike back to the lighthouse in Cabo de Gata). Bicycle to Aguadulce. Go out and enjoy the nightlife, Almería has a bunch of clubs in the city center (a lot with reggaeton but also some that plays techno - check out Palo Santo for that, or keep an eye out for events in Complejo Chaman/Chain Club which is located a bit outside the city). For bars I'd recommend Kutre, which is a fun place. In general, keep an eye out for festivals (Solazo fest in spring/summer) and concerts taking place in and outside the city. You also have the possibility to go outside the city for weekend trips - to Malaga, Granada (but book tickets for Alhambra some weeks in advance) and Sevilla. There are buses that connect the cities but a lot of times it's much easier and faster to go with blablacar.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy. It's different to Denmark but more in a way that revolves around the weather and dinner times, so I didn't find it hard to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It's difficult if you don't know Spanish. If you do, you can definitely talk to them after class or sit down next to someone in class. In some subjects you have to do group work with them which is a good opportunity to get to talk. In general, they're were sweet and willing to talk if you start the conversation. But a lot of them have had their friends and their class for years and might not be too interested in getting to know new people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The challenges were definitely more about the ways of teaching in the uni and the bigger workload than differences in culture.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I think the whole vibe is more chill and relaxing. The locals are not as busy (or maybe they are, they're just not acting as busy) as the people that live in Copenhagen. This was a big plus for me. People are really sweet and welcoming and not afraid to talk to strangers.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Just do it honestly. It's an amazing opportunity to go somewhere completely new and exciting to just study and make new friends (and the erasmus grant is a big economic support). It's going to be scary and confusing at first but it WILL get better and easier and in the end you'll be so happy you did it. 

2) If you're there to learn the language, it doesn't come by itself just because you're staying in Spain. It definitely helps listening to Spanish all the time, going to class etc., but you also have to speak to native Spanish speakers. It can be really scary but the more you do it, the less scary it will be. Just remember that people don't see you as stupid if you make mistakes - they see it as amazing that you're able to say and understand someting in their language. 

3) Enjoy all the things outside of uni as much as possible. Even if you have a lot of stuff to do for uni, try to make time to have fun. I was surprised about the good grades most of my teachers gave in the end - don't worry too much about not passing. If you're in doubt, ask some of your class mates in the beginning (preferably before changing to the subject for good) about the level of the different subjects you're about to choose. Some of them have taken the subjects before or know someone that has, and they can give you an idea of the expectations.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
- Go on idealista to find accommodation (and face time with your land lord before if possible) and 
- Ask the teacher about the chances of passing the subject as an erasmus student before choosing their subject
- Ask your teacher about bringing a dictionary to the exams
- Choose classes that are scheduled during the day
- Try to go to class as much as possible, the exams will be so much easier in the end. And it's nice to have an everyday life with classes during the day and to be off during the afternoon/nights. 
- Take notes in class, just write everything (that you possibly can) that the teacher says. Ask your class mates for notes and use the website wuolah when studying for the exams
- Ask your class mates to add you in the whatsapp group in every subject. Every subjects has their own chat group in which changes in timetable, homework etc. will be written
- Go to the emergency room in the public hospital if you get sick. It's free with the blue health card

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting better at the language, meeting a bunch of amazing people that I would like to visit in their home countries and in general just living in a place where the sun (almost) always shines (when it's not crazy windy which it is sometimes in Almería) and where you can always go to the beach or out for dinner or tapas without paying a lot.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Overall, it all went really well. If I were to change something, I would have pushed myself more to talk with native Spanish speakers. It can be hard in the beginning if you don't feel like your level is that good (but it will get better though no matter what).

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
